screens.title: Data Migration Services
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the AWS services you will use when moving data into or out of AWS. You will learn when to choose a physical transport device versus an automated network transfer, and how managed file-transfer endpoints and database migration tooling reduce operational risk. Start by understanding the Snow Family for offline large-scale work: Snowcone, Snowball Edge, and Snowmobile each solve different scales and connectivity scenarios. Then we’ll look at DataSync for efficient online transfers between NFS, SMB or object storage and AWS, and Transfer Family for protocol-based uploads to S3 or EFS. We also cover the Database Migration Service for moving live databases with minimal downtime. Why this matters: picking the wrong tool can inflate costs, lengthen migrations, and create security gaps. A common real-world example is a media archive of tens of terabytes where shipping a Snowball Edge can be faster and cheaper than trying to push data over a constrained network. By the end you will be able to match dataset size, bandwidth, and transfer frequency to the right AWS service and frame the security and cost trade-offs. Consider this a practical checklist you can apply during a migration decision.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Data Migration Services
Data Migration Services
Move data reliably between on-premises and AWS across many scales and protocols.

You’ll learn when to ship data physically, when to accelerate transfers over the network, and how to provide secure protocol endpoints for partners and legacy tools. Practical trade-offs include speed, cost, and security.

Concept map
Snow Family • DataSync • Transfer Family • DMS
Snowcone — portable 8 TB
Snowball Edge — 80–100 TB storage or compute
Snowmobile — 100 PB truck-scale transfer
Explore Key Topics
Snow Family — offline devices to bypass bandwidth limits.
DataSync — optimized, automated online transfers and scheduling.
Transfer Family — managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints into S3/EFS.
Coming up: device scales, an on-premises DataSync walkthrough, and how to choose the right service for your constraints.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In these objectives we set clear, measurable outcomes so you can apply migration choices with confidence. First, you will identify when to use the Snow Family devices — from Snowcone for small edge jobs to Snowmobile for exabyte-scale transfers. That matters because choosing a physical device can avoid long network transfer times and unexpected costs. Second, you will explain how DataSync moves data efficiently across networks, including its agent, accelerated protocol, and integrity checks. This matters for recurring syncs and one-time migrations where you need automation and reliability. Third, you will describe AWS Transfer Family and how it provides managed SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints directly into S3 or EFS, removing the need to operate your own file servers. That matters when partners or legacy systems require standard protocols. Finally, you will learn to choose the best migration tool based on dataset size, bandwidth, frequency, protocol requirements, and downtime tolerance. Each objective ties to practical scenarios such as a 75-terabyte archive transfer or enabling partner uploads via SFTP. These competencies prepare you to propose safe, cost-conscious migration plans.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Security & Cost
Security, cost, and decision criteria
Practical checks to validate migration choices against governance and budget.
Security
  • Snow devices use tamper-resistant enclosures and 256-bit encryption.
  • DataSync handles encryption and integrity checks during transfer.
  • Transfer Family integrates with IAM and directory providers for access control.
Cost drivers
  • Device rental and shipping for Snow devices.
  • Network egress or long-running transfer time costs for online moves.
  • Managed endpoint and per-user costs for Transfer Family.
Decision checklist
  1. Estimate data volume and transfer window.
  2. Check network bandwidth and reliability.
  3. Confirm protocol and downtime requirements.
Key Takeaway

You must weigh security, speed, and cost together. For large volumes with poor bandwidth, offline Snow devices often beat network transfers.

screens.title: The Snow Family — when physical shipment wins
screens.narratorSegment: The Snow Family provides physical data transfer devices designed to move very large datasets when networks are too slow, unreliable, or costly. Think of these devices as trusted couriers for your data: AWS ships a rugged device to your location, you load data locally, then return the device and AWS ingests the content into S3. This pattern eliminates the network as the primary bottleneck. A concrete example from the chapter: moving 75 terabytes over a 200 megabit-per-second upload would take many weeks. Renting a Snowball Edge with eighty to one hundred terabytes of usable storage and shipping it is often faster and more cost-effective for that scale. A common misconception is that physical devices are inherently insecure. The Snow Family uses tamper-resistant enclosures, 256-bit encryption, and chain-of-custody tracking to maintain security and compliance during transit. Another contrast is between Snowcone and Snowball Edge: Snowcone is portable with about eight terabytes of usable storage and suits edge collection or small transfers, while Snowball Edge offers much larger capacity and optional compute for pre-processing at the edge. Snowmobile sits at the extreme end: for entire data centers, a truck-scale container can move up to one hundred petabytes. When planning, always compare device capacity and shipment time to your available network transfer rate and your deadline.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Snow Family
The Snow Family — when physical shipment wins
Devices bypass network limits to move very large datasets securely.
Definitions & comparison
Snowcone — portable, 8 TB usable storage. Edge collection and small transfers.
Snowball Edge — Storage or compute optimized. 80–100 TB usable storage; can run EC2/Lambda.
Snowmobile — Truck-scale container up to 100 PB. For migrating entire data centers.
Security note

Devices use tamper-resistant enclosures, 256-bit encryption, and chain-of-custody tracking during shipment.

Concrete scenario
Scenario: You have 75 TB of archived video and a 200 Mbps upload link. Network transfer will take far longer than your migration window. Selecting a Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device will let you copy data locally and ship it back to AWS, completing the migration within your timeframe.
Misconception
Some teams assume shipping is insecure or slow. In reality, Snow devices offer strong encryption and are often faster for very large volumes when network constraints apply.
Key Takeaway

If your transfer window and bandwidth can’t move the data on time, shipping a Snow device is frequently the fastest and most predictable choice.

screens.title: Snowcone in detail — edge and portable transfers
screens.narratorSegment: Snowcone is the smallest Snow Family device. It provides around eight terabytes of usable storage in a rugged, portable package that you can carry to disconnected or harsh environments. Use Snowcone for edge data collection, small-scale migrations, or when you need to run lightweight compute at the edge. Snowcone supports running EC2 instances and AWS IoT Greengrass for local processing, which lets you filter or summarize data before shipment and reduce the amount of data you need to move. A concrete example is a remote field site collecting sensor logs where local preprocessing filters out noise and only the aggregated results are shipped. A common misconception is expecting Snowcone to be a full replacement for larger Snowball Edge devices; it is intentionally limited in capacity and compute. When your dataset grows beyond single-digit terabytes or when you require G P U-enabled compute, Snowball Edge or Snowmobile are the appropriate next steps. When choosing Snowcone, validate your edge compute needs and whether local processing can reduce transfer volume enough to justify the device rental and shipping time. Snowcone in detail — edge and portable transfers means portable edge collection and lightweight local processing; good when data is small and connectivity is limited.. In practical terms, what snowcone is best for and its processing capabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Snowcone
Snowcone in detail — edge and portable transfers
Small, rugged, and useful where connectivity is limited.
Capabilities
  • Approximately 8 TB usable storage for data collection.
  • Runs EC2 instances and AWS IoT Greengrass for light edge compute.
  • Portable and designed for disconnected or harsh locations.
Analogy
Think of Snowcone as a hardened USB drive with local compute — it collects, pre-processes, and ships a compact dataset to the cloud.
Concrete example
A remote environmental sensor array uses Snowcone to locally aggregate measurements and discard noisy samples. The operator then returns the device for ingestion into S3, reducing network transfer needs.
Misconception
Snowcone is not intended to replace high-capacity Snowball Edge devices; it is optimized for portability and local processing on small datasets.
Key Takeaway

Choose Snowcone when you need portability, local processing, and only a few terabytes of data moved from a disconnected site.

screens.title: Snowball Edge — storage vs compute optimized
screens.narratorSegment: Snowball Edge comes in two main options: storage optimized and compute optimized. The storage optimized device provides eighty to one hundred terabytes of usable storage and is ideal when you need to move large collections of files or objects. The compute optimized variant offers around forty-two terabytes of usable storage but includes additional vCPUs and optional G P U resources for heavier edge processing. Both options can run EC2 instances and Lambda functions locally, so you can preprocess, filter, or analyze data before shipping it back to AWS. This is useful in scenarios where moving raw data is expensive or slow, and running compute at the edge reduces the volume to be transferred. A common decision point is whether your migration requires pre-processing: if so, prefer compute optimized; if you simply need bulk capacity, choose storage optimized. Another common misconception is assuming both options only act as dumb storage. In practice, the ability to run compute locally can reduce overall transfer time and costs by eliminating unneeded data before shipping. Always validate the runtime requirements for your edge workloads before selecting a flavor.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Snowball Edge
Snowball Edge — storage vs compute optimized
Choose based on whether you need capacity or local processing at scale.
Storage Optimized
Offers 80 TB or 100 TB usable storage. Ideal for large-scale bulk transfers when compute at the edge is minimal or unnecessary.
Best for
Archival moves, bulk dataset consolidation, or when you need maximum usable capacity per device.
Compute Optimized
Provides about 42 TB usable storage but more vCPUs and optional GPUs. Run EC2 or Lambda to process data before shipping.
Best for
Pre-processing, filtering, encoding, or running ML inference at the edge to shrink transferred data.
Concrete example: A media processing pipeline that transcodes raw footage at the edge and uploads only the compressed results can use a compute optimized Snowball Edge to reduce the transfer volume by orders of magnitude.
Key Takeaway

Select storage optimized for capacity and compute optimized when local processing will reduce the data you send back to AWS.

screens.title: Snowmobile — extreme scale migrations
screens.narratorSegment: Snowmobile addresses the rare but critical need to move extremely large datasets, such as whole data centers, to AWS. It uses a 45-foot ruggedized shipping container transported by truck and can move up to one hundred petabytes per snowmobile. This option is reserved for migrations at exabyte scale or for organizations that have many data center racks to consolidate. Use Snowmobile when incremental network transfer is not feasible due to sheer volume or when regulatory or physical constraints favor a single predictable migration window. A misconception to avoid is using Snowmobile for every large transfer; the service is specialized and typically invoked only when your volume far exceeds Snowball Edge capacity. When evaluating Snowmobile, compare the logistics, security chain-of-custody, and the time to stage and load the container versus parallel network strategies or multiple Snowball devices. In many cases, a combination of appliance shipments and online transfers provides the best balance between speed and cost. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Snowmobile
Snowmobile — extreme scale migrations
A truck-scale container for moving tens to hundreds of petabytes.
What it is
A 45-foot ruggedized container transported by semi-trailer, designed to move exceptionally large datasets up to 100 PB per unit.
When to consider
  • Entire data center consolidation.
  • Exabyte-scale archives that cannot be moved practically over the network.
Planning tips
Validate logistics, staging area capacity, security and chain-of-custody, and plan how to load and verify data before unit pickup and AWS ingestion.
Misconception
Snowmobile is not a default choice for large moves; it is reserved for extreme scale where other approaches are insufficient.
Key Takeaway

Use Snowmobile only when your migration volume and timeline make it the most practical option; otherwise prefer Snowball Edge or hybrid approaches.

screens.title: Snow Family secure workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Migrating with a Snow device follows a predictable secure workflow that minimizes exposure and preserves data integrity. First, request the device from the cloud provider and plan shipping and staging logistics. Next, the device arrives with a tamper-resistant enclosure; you mount the device on your local network and copy data into its storage. While copying, ensure local encryption at rest and follow your chain-of-custody procedures; Snow devices use 256-bit encryption, and AWS tracks custody for compliance. After copying, validate the data and prepare the device for pickup. Ship the device back to AWS for ingestion into S3. Finally, verify the data in S3 and securely erase the device storage as required. A common misconception is that this is a casual lift-and-ship process. In reality, you must plan bandwidth for local copies, allocate time for validation, and follow security controls to preserve auditability. For example, teams handling regulated data should document chain-of-custody events and coordinate with their compliance teams prior to device receipt and return. The central insight: plan each step and treat the device as a controlled asset rather than a disposable drive.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Snow Workflow
Snow Family secure workflow
Planable, auditable steps to keep data secure during physical transfer.
Process
1. Request device
2. Ship and stage
3. Copy & encrypt
4. Validate & return
5. Ingest & verify
  • Use tamper-resistant enclosures and 256-bit encryption for data at rest.
  • Perform integrity checks after copying and before shipping.
  • Document chain-of-custody events for compliance.
Concrete note
Treat the device like a controlled asset. Plan staging space, validation time, and responsible custody handoffs to avoid delays and audit issues.
Check
Have a checklist for pre-shipment validation and post-ingest verification to avoid rework.

screens.title: AWS DataSync — online transfer at scale
screens.narratorSegment: AWS DataSync is an online transfer service that automates and accelerates moving data between on-premises storage and AWS. It uses a lightweight agent you deploy on-premises to read and write files from NFS, SMB, or self-managed object stores, and transfers them to S3, EFS, or FSx. DataSync is built for reliability: it uses an optimized transfer protocol, handles network interruptions, performs integrity verification, and supports bandwidth limits and scheduling. A concrete example is migrating petabytes of data from an on-premises NFS server to S3 using a DataSync task. You deploy an agent in your data center, register source and destination locations in the console, configure a task, and run it. A common misconception is treating DataSync as a simple file copy; in fact it provides filters, bandwidth controls, and integrity checks that make large migrations predictable and safe. DataSync is also handy for recurring synchronization and disaster recovery. When designing with DataSync, plan agent placement for network proximity to sources, configure an IAM role to allow writes to destination storage, and consider incremental sync schedules to reduce transfer load. This balances speed, cost, and operational simplicity.

keyIdea.text: Deploy an agent, register locations, configure tasks and schedules; DataSync automates optimized, reliable transfers from NFS/SMB/object stores to S3/EFS/FSx.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › DataSync
AWS DataSync — online transfer at scale
Agent-based, optimized transfer for file and object data into AWS storage.
Architecture overview
DataSync uses an on-premises agent that connects securely to the DataSync service and streams data to S3, EFS, or FSx. The agent reads source locations like NFS or SMB and writes to the target with integrity verification and optional bandwidth limits.
Capabilities
  • Optimized transfer protocol and retry handling.
  • Data integrity verification and scheduling.
  • Support for filters, bandwidth limits, and IAM roles.
Concrete walkthrough (conceptual)
Create an S3 bucket, deploy the DataSync agent on-premises, register the NFS source and S3 destination, configure a task (transfer all data and verify integrity), and start or schedule the task.
Misconception
Do not assume DataSync is just a manual copy. It gives automation, retries, integrity checks and scheduling that are essential for predictable large transfers.
Key Takeaway

Use DataSync when you have reliable network connectivity and you need automated, verifiable transfers between on-premises shares and AWS storage.

screens.title: DataSync conceptual walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through the conceptual steps to set up a DataSync task. The goal is not to run commands here, but to understand the required pieces and configuration choices. Step one: create a destination S3 bucket to receive data. Name it clearly so other teams recognize it. Step two: deploy a DataSync agent in your on-premises environment on a VM that has network access to the NFS or SMB share. Activate the agent in the DataSync console so the service can communicate with it. Step three: register a source location in the console and provide the NFS server IP and the mount path. Step four: register an S3 destination and attach an IAM role that grants DataSync write access to the chosen bucket. DataSync conceptual walkthrough
Understand the console steps and configuration checks you must make.
Checklist

screens.title: AWS Transfer Family — managed protocol endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Transfer Family provides fully managed endpoints that let clients use SFTP, FTPS, or FTP to move files directly into S3 or EFS. This removes the operational burden of running and patching your own protocol servers. Transfer Family integrates with IAM, Active Directory, LDAP, or custom identity providers, so you can control which users have access to which buckets or file systems. A concrete scenario from the chapter: a software vendor wants customers to upload large log files from various SFTP clients into an S3 bucket for analysis, and prefers not to manage the SFTP servers themselves. Transfer Family is the right fit because it offers a highly available, scalable endpoint that maps protocol users to storage locations. A common mistake is continuing to maintain custom SFTP infrastructure when a managed endpoint would reduce operational risk and simplify access control. When designing, choose the correct endpoint type (for example, publicly accessible or VPC hosted), pick an identity provider, set home directories to limit access scope, and add users with appropriate authentication keys. The key insight: Transfer Family reduces operational overhead while preserving compatibility with industry-standard transfer tools.

Example scenario
A vendor offers an SFTP endpoint so customers can upload log files directly into S3. Transfer Family provides the endpoint, scales for availability, and integrates with IAM so each customer only accesses their folder.

Running your own SFTP server is not necessary in many cases; managed endpoints reduce patching and availability concerns.

screens.narratorSegment: This conceptual setup outlines how you would create a Transfer Family server and allow a user to upload files into S3. Step one: create a server in Transfer Family and choose the protocol, for example SFTP. Choose the endpoint type — publicly accessible for broad partner access, or VPC for restricted internal networks. Step two: select an identity provider such as service-managed users or an Active Directory integration depending on your authentication needs. Step three: configure the S3 bucket you will use as the user’s home directory and attach appropriate IAM permissions so Transfer Family can write into that path. screens.title: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Database Migration Service helps you move relational and NoSQL databases to AWS with minimal downtime. DMS supports homogeneous migrations, where source and target engines are the same, and heterogeneous migrations, where you change engines — for example moving from an on-premises database to Amazon Aurora. A key capability of DMS is continuous data replication, which keeps source and target synchronized during the cutover window and reduces application downtime. Use DMS for migrating production databases, consolidating data stores, or seeding an analytics platform. A common misconception is that DMS handles full schema conversions automatically; while DMS migrates data and can replicate changes, heterogeneous migrations often require additional schema and application changes handled by complementary tools. When planning, verify supported source and target engines, size replication instances appropriately, and plan a cutover window with validation. The practical question to ask is how much continuous replication you need to minimize downtime and whether any application-level changes are required for the target engine. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) means use dms to migrate and continuously replicate databases with minimal downtime; heterogeneous migrations may need additional schema conversion work.. In practical terms, migrate databases with minimal downtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)
Move databases to AWS with continuous replication and reduced downtime.
Capabilities
  • Supports relational and NoSQL sources to various AWS targets.

  • Supports homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations.
Planning notes
Confirm engine compatibility, prepare schema conversion if changing engines, size replication instances for throughput, and validate replication with test data before cutover.

DMS migrates data and changes but complex schema transformations for heterogeneous targets may require additional tooling and testing.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing the chapter, keep these core concepts top of mind. First, the Snow Family provides physical transfer devices that bypass network limits: Snowcone for portable edge use, Snowball Edge for large-scale storage or compute-enabled edge processing, and Snowmobile for exabyte-scale migrations. Second, DataSync automates and accelerates online transfers between on-premises NFS/SMB/object stores and AWS storage, handling retries, integrity checks, and bandwidth controls. Third, Transfer Family gives you managed SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints that integrate with S3 or EFS and with your identity systems, reducing operational overhead for protocol-based file exchange. Finally, DMS helps migrate databases with continuous replication to minimize downtime, though heterogeneous migrations often need additional schema work. These services address complementary migration problems: physical shipment for poor bandwidth or huge volumes, agent-driven transfers for robust network migrations, protocol gateways for partner integration, and database replication for live systems. When planning any migration, evaluate data volume, bandwidth, transfer frequency, protocol needs, downtime tolerance, security, and cost to choose the right service combination.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Quick Memory
What to Remember
Three compact reminders to guide migration choices.
Volume vs Bandwidth
High volume with low bandwidth favors Snow devices; low volume or fast links favor DataSync or direct network transfer.
Managed over DIY
Use DataSync and Transfer Family to reduce server management, improve availability, and simplify security.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the AWS services you will use when moving data into or out of AWS. You will learn when to choose a physical transport device versus an automated network transfer, and how managed file-transfer endpoints and database migration tooling reduce operational risk. Start by understanding the Snow Family for offline large-scale work: Snowcone, Snowball Edge, and Snowmobile each solve different scales and connectivity scenarios. Then we’ll look at DataSync for efficient online transfers between NFS, SMB or object storage and AWS, and Transfer Family for protocol-based uploads to S3 or EFS. We also cover the Database Migration Service for moving live databases with minimal downtime. Why this matters: picking the wrong tool can inflate costs, lengthen migrations, and create security gaps. A common real-world example is a media archive of tens of terabytes where shipping a Snowball Edge can be faster and cheaper than trying to push data over a constrained network. By the end you will be able to match dataset size, bandwidth, and transfer frequency to the right AWS service and frame the security and cost trade-offs. Consider this a practical checklist you can apply during a migration decision.

In these objectives we set clear, measurable outcomes so you can apply migration choices with confidence. First, you will identify when to use the Snow Family devices — from Snowcone for small edge jobs to Snowmobile for exabyte-scale transfers. That matters because choosing a physical device can avoid long network transfer times and unexpected costs. Second, you will explain how DataSync moves data efficiently across networks, including its agent, accelerated protocol, and integrity checks. This matters for recurring syncs and one-time migrations where you need automation and reliability. Third, you will describe AWS Transfer Family and how it provides managed SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints directly into S3 or EFS, removing the need to operate your own file servers. That matters when partners or legacy systems require standard protocols. Finally, you will learn to choose the best migration tool based on dataset size, bandwidth, frequency, protocol requirements, and downtime tolerance. Each objective ties to practical scenarios such as a 75-terabyte archive transfer or enabling partner uploads via SFTP. These competencies prepare you to propose safe, cost-conscious migration plans.

This second objectives slide focuses on the constraints and guardrails you will use during planning. You will understand security and compliance measures for migration services, such as encryption, tamper-resistant enclosures, and identity integration. Knowing these controls matters because audits and data governance determine whether an approach is acceptable. Next, you will estimate cost drivers — device rental and shipping for Snow, network costs for online transfers, and managed endpoint pricing for Transfer Family — so you can build realistic migration budgets. Third, you will practice mapping protocol requirements to services: NFS/SMB/object storage with DataSync, SFTP/FTPS/FTP with Transfer Family, and database engines with Database Migration Service. Finally, you will practice a migration decision process that balances data volume, bandwidth, transfer frequency, downtime tolerance, and protocol constraints. A short scenario to anchor this: when internet bandwidth is low and downtime tolerance is limited, shipping a Snowball Edge can be faster and less expensive than a network transfer. These competencies reduce surprise delays and expense during actual migrations.

The Snow Family provides physical data transfer devices designed to move very large datasets when networks are too slow, unreliable, or costly. Think of these devices as trusted couriers for your data: AWS ships a rugged device to your location, you load data locally, then return the device and AWS ingests the content into S3. This pattern eliminates the network as the primary bottleneck. A concrete example from the chapter: moving 75 terabytes over a 200 megabit-per-second upload would take many weeks. Renting a Snowball Edge with eighty to one hundred terabytes of usable storage and shipping it is often faster and more cost-effective for that scale. A common misconception is that physical devices are inherently insecure. The Snow Family uses tamper-resistant enclosures, 256-bit encryption, and chain-of-custody tracking to maintain security and compliance during transit. Another contrast is between Snowcone and Snowball Edge: Snowcone is portable with about eight terabytes of usable storage and suits edge collection or small transfers, while Snowball Edge offers much larger capacity and optional compute for pre-processing at the edge. Snowmobile sits at the extreme end: for entire data centers, a truck-scale container can move up to one hundred petabytes. When planning, always compare device capacity and shipment time to your available network transfer rate and your deadline.

Snowcone is the smallest Snow Family device. It provides around eight terabytes of usable storage in a rugged, portable package that you can carry to disconnected or harsh environments. Use Snowcone for edge data collection, small-scale migrations, or when you need to run lightweight compute at the edge. Snowcone supports running EC2 instances and AWS IoT Greengrass for local processing, which lets you filter or summarize data before shipment and reduce the amount of data you need to move. A concrete example is a remote field site collecting sensor logs where local preprocessing filters out noise and only the aggregated results are shipped. A common misconception is expecting Snowcone to be a full replacement for larger Snowball Edge devices; it is intentionally limited in capacity and compute. When your dataset grows beyond single-digit terabytes or when you require G P U-enabled compute, Snowball Edge or Snowmobile are the appropriate next steps. When choosing Snowcone, validate your edge compute needs and whether local processing can reduce transfer volume enough to justify the device rental and shipping time. Snowcone in detail — edge and portable transfers means portable edge collection and lightweight local processing; good when data is small and connectivity is limited.. In practical terms, what snowcone is best for and its processing capabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Snowball Edge comes in two main options: storage optimized and compute optimized. The storage optimized device provides eighty to one hundred terabytes of usable storage and is ideal when you need to move large collections of files or objects. The compute optimized variant offers around forty-two terabytes of usable storage but includes additional vCPUs and optional G P U resources for heavier edge processing. Both options can run EC2 instances and Lambda functions locally, so you can preprocess, filter, or analyze data before shipping it back to AWS. This is useful in scenarios where moving raw data is expensive or slow, and running compute at the edge reduces the volume to be transferred. A common decision point is whether your migration requires pre-processing: if so, prefer compute optimized; if you simply need bulk capacity, choose storage optimized. Another common misconception is assuming both options only act as dumb storage. In practice, the ability to run compute locally can reduce overall transfer time and costs by eliminating unneeded data before shipping. Always validate the runtime requirements for your edge workloads before selecting a flavor.

Snowmobile addresses the rare but critical need to move extremely large datasets, such as whole data centers, to AWS. It uses a 45-foot ruggedized shipping container transported by truck and can move up to one hundred petabytes per snowmobile. This option is reserved for migrations at exabyte scale or for organizations that have many data center racks to consolidate. Use Snowmobile when incremental network transfer is not feasible due to sheer volume or when regulatory or physical constraints favor a single predictable migration window. A misconception to avoid is using Snowmobile for every large transfer; the service is specialized and typically invoked only when your volume far exceeds Snowball Edge capacity. When evaluating Snowmobile, compare the logistics, security chain-of-custody, and the time to stage and load the container versus parallel network strategies or multiple Snowball devices. In many cases, a combination of appliance shipments and online transfers provides the best balance between speed and cost. Migrating with a Snow device follows a predictable secure workflow that minimizes exposure and preserves data integrity. First, request the device from the cloud provider and plan shipping and staging logistics. Next, the device arrives with a tamper-resistant enclosure; you mount the device on your local network and copy data into its storage. While copying, ensure local encryption at rest and follow your chain-of-custody procedures; Snow devices use 256-bit encryption, and AWS tracks custody for compliance. After copying, validate the data and prepare the device for pickup. Ship the device back to AWS for ingestion into S3. Finally, verify the data in S3 and securely erase the device storage as required. A common misconception is that this is a casual lift-and-ship process. In reality, you must plan bandwidth for local copies, allocate time for validation, and follow security controls to preserve auditability. For example, teams handling regulated data should document chain-of-custody events and coordinate with their compliance teams prior to device receipt and return. The central insight: plan each step and treat the device as a controlled asset rather than a disposable drive.

Summarizing the chapter, keep these core concepts top of mind. First, the Snow Family provides physical transfer devices that bypass network limits: Snowcone for portable edge use, Snowball Edge for large-scale storage or compute-enabled edge processing, and Snowmobile for exabyte-scale migrations. Second, DataSync automates and accelerates online transfers between on-premises NFS/SMB/object stores and AWS storage, handling retries, integrity checks, and bandwidth controls. Third, Transfer Family gives you managed SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints that integrate with S3 or EFS and with your identity systems, reducing operational overhead for protocol-based file exchange. Finally, DMS helps migrate databases with continuous replication to minimize downtime, though heterogeneous migrations often need additional schema work. These services address complementary migration problems: physical shipment for poor bandwidth or huge volumes, agent-driven transfers for robust network migrations, protocol gateways for partner integration, and database replication for live systems. When planning any migration, evaluate data volume, bandwidth, transfer frequency, protocol needs, downtime tolerance, security, and cost to choose the right service combination.
